sets.title: Old town photos wanted
sets.passage: The Stelbridge library is planning a show about our town in the past, and we need your help. Do you have photographs of Stelbridge that were taken before 1980? Please bring them to the local history room on any Saturday morning in March. A librarian will scan each photo while you wait, and you will take your originals home with you the same day. The copies will hang in the main hall from April. If you know the year or the place, please write it on the back of each photo.

choices: to ask people to give their old town photos to the library
to ask people to take new town photos for a library show
to ask people to lend their old town photos for copying
to tell people that a show of old town photos is now open
items.correct_answer: to ask people to lend their old town photos for copying
items.why: A librarian will scan each photo while you wait
items.explanation: "to ask people to lend their old town photos for copying" is correct: the notice asks readers to "bring them to the local history room", where "A librarian will scan each photo while you wait", and the owners keep the originals, so the photos are lent and copied.

distractor_rationales.choice: to ask people to give their old town photos to the library
distractor_rationales.reason: "to ask people to give their old town photos to the library" is wrong: the photos are only scanned, and "you will take your originals home with you the same day".

distractor_rationales.choice: to ask people to take new town photos for a library show
distractor_rationales.reason: "to ask people to take new town photos for a library show" is wrong: the library wants photographs "that were taken before 1980", not new ones.

distractor_rationales.choice: to tell people that a show of old town photos is now open
distractor_rationales.reason: "to tell people that a show of old town photos is now open" is wrong: the library "is planning a show", and "The copies will hang in the main hall from April", so the show has not opened yet.

sets.title: Borrowing a tripod
sets.passage:
Hi Tuva,

Thanks for showing me your camera on Friday. My group has to film a short video about the school garden for science class, and my phone keeps shaking in my hands. Could I borrow your tripod? I can pick it up from your house on Saturday after my piano lesson, at about two o'clock. We plan to film on Sunday afternoon. I will bring the tripod back to school on Monday morning, before first period.

See you soon,
Zora

items.prompt: When does Zora say she will return the tripod?
choices: on Saturday, after her piano lesson ends
on Sunday, after her group films the video
on Friday, after she sees Tuva's camera
on Monday, before lessons start at school
items.correct_answer: on Monday, before lessons start at school
items.why: I will bring the tripod back to school on Monday morning, before first period
items.explanation: "on Monday, before lessons start at school" is correct: Zora writes "I will bring the tripod back to school on Monday morning, before first period", which is before lessons start.

distractor_rationales.choice: on Saturday, after her piano lesson ends
distractor_rationales.reason: "on Saturday, after her piano lesson ends" is wrong: Saturday after the piano lesson is when she will "pick it up from your house", not return it.

distractor_rationales.choice: on Sunday, after her group films the video
distractor_rationales.reason: "on Sunday, after her group films the video" is wrong: Sunday is only when "We plan to film"; she says "I will bring the tripod back to school on Monday morning".

distractor_rationales.choice: on Friday, after she sees Tuva's camera
distractor_rationales.reason: "on Friday, after she sees Tuva's camera" is wrong: Friday is in the past, when Tuva was "showing me your camera on Friday"; the tripod comes back "on Monday morning".

sets.title: The iron at the class museum
sets.passage:
In October, our history teacher, Ms. Vandell, told us that our class would turn our classroom into a museum for one day. Each of us had to bring an everyday object that was at least fifty years old and write a short label explaining how it was used.

I borrowed my grandmother's old iron. It was black, heavy and a little rusty, and it had to be heated on a stove before anyone could use it. Next to Talvi's painted music box, which played a tune when you opened it, my iron looked boring, and I almost left it in my bag.

My grandmother helped me with the label. She told me that she pressed her school uniform with the iron every Sunday night. She also told me that she once burned her best blouse because she forgot to test the heat on an old cloth first. I wrote both stories on the card in my neatest handwriting.

On museum day, the music box got a few smiles, but the iron got questions. Younger students tried to lift it with one hand and laughed when they could not. A father asked how anyone kept the heat even. Two teachers read my label twice.

That evening I gave the iron back to my grandmother and told her about every visitor. She listened carefully. Then she asked whether she could come to the next museum day herself.

items.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: how everyday objects from long ago can still interest young people today
how younger students tried to lift a heavy old iron at a class museum
how an object the writer thought was dull drew interest at a class museum
how an object the writer was proud of was ignored at a class museum
items.correct_answer: how an object the writer thought was dull drew interest at a class museum
items.why: my iron looked boring, and I almost left it in my bag
items.explanation: "how an object the writer thought was dull drew interest at a class museum" is correct: the writer first says "my iron looked boring, and I almost left it in my bag", but on museum day "the iron got questions", and she later "told her about every visitor".

distractor_rationales.choice: how everyday objects from long ago can still interest young people today
distractor_rationales.reason: "how everyday objects from long ago can still interest young people today" is too general: the passage is about one class museum and one object, the iron that "looked boring" to the writer and then "got questions".

distractor_rationales.choice: how younger students tried to lift a heavy old iron at a class museum
distractor_rationales.reason: "how younger students tried to lift a heavy old iron at a class museum" is only one detail from paragraph 4 ("Younger students tried to lift it with one hand"), not the whole passage.

distractor_rationales.choice: how an object the writer was proud of was ignored at a class museum
distractor_rationales.reason: "how an object the writer was proud of was ignored at a class museum" gets the story backwards: the writer first thought "my iron looked boring", and on the day "the iron got questions".

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, the word "pressed" is closest in meaning to
choices: pushed
insisted
squeezed
smoothed
items.why: she pressed her school uniform with the iron every Sunday night
items.explanation: "smoothed" is correct: an iron "had to be heated on a stove" and is used on clothes, so when she "pressed her school uniform with the iron" she made it smooth and flat.

distractor_rationales.choice: pushed
distractor_rationales.reason: "pushed" is another meaning of the word, but the grandmother used an iron on clothes: she "pressed her school uniform with the iron", which makes cloth flat, not moved.

distractor_rationales.choice: insisted
distractor_rationales.reason: "insisted" means to keep asking a person firmly for something; a uniform is a thing, and she "pressed her school uniform with the iron".

distractor_rationales.choice: squeezed
distractor_rationales.reason: "squeezed" is used for fruit or hands; an iron heated "on a stove" is used to flatten cloth, as when she "pressed her school uniform with the iron".

choices: to show why the writer's own object seemed boring to her
to show which object got the most questions on museum day

to show what kind of object Ms. Vandell had asked them to bring

items.explanation: "to show why the writer's own object seemed boring to her" is correct: the writer says "Next to Talvi's painted music box, which played a tune when you opened it, my iron looked boring", so the music box is mentioned as a comparison.

distractor_rationales.choice: to show which object got the most questions on museum day
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show which object got the most questions on museum day" is wrong: on museum day "the music box got a few smiles, but the iron got questions".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show which object the writer had first planned to bring
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show which object the writer had first planned to bring" is wrong: the music box is "Talvi's painted music box", and the writer says "I borrowed my grandmother's old iron".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show what kind of object Ms. Vandell had asked them to bring
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show what kind of object Ms. Vandell had asked them to bring" is wrong: the teacher's instruction is given in paragraph 1, "an everyday object that was at least fifty years old", and the music box appears only as the thing beside which "my iron looked boring".

items.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the label the writer made for the iron?
choices: It was written by the grandmother in her own handwriting.
It told about a mistake the grandmother once made with the iron.

items.correct_answer: It told about a mistake the grandmother once made with the iron.
items.why: she once burned her best blouse because she forgot to test the heat on an old cloth first
items.why2: I wrote both stories on the card in my neatest handwriting

distractor_rationales.choice: It was written by the grandmother in her own handwriting.
distractor_rationales.reason: "It was written by the grandmother in her own handwriting." is contradicted: the writer says "I wrote both stories on the card in my neatest handwriting".

distractor_rationales.choice: It said the grandmother used the iron every Saturday morning.
distractor_rationales.reason: "It said the grandmother used the iron every Saturday morning." is contradicted: the grandmother "pressed her school uniform with the iron every Sunday night".

distractor_rationales.reason: "It told visitors that the iron was heated by electricity." is contradicted: the iron "had to be heated on a stove before anyone could use it".

sets.title: From hot wires to LEDs
sets.passage:
For more than a century, the ordinary light bulb was really a small heater that happened to glow. Inside the glass, an electric current passed through a thin wire called a filament, usually made of the metal tungsten. The wire became so hot, well over two thousand degrees, that it gave off light. Yet most of the energy, roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat rather than as visible light. Anyone who has touched a lamp that was switched on an hour earlier has learned this quickly.

The filament also limited how long a bulb could work. At such high temperatures, tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire, so the filament became thinner in places until it finally broke. A typical bulb lasted about a thousand hours, which is why changing bulbs was once a regular household chore.

Light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, work in a completely different way. An LED is a tiny piece of specially prepared material, called a semiconductor, through which electricity flows. As the current moves through it, energy is released directly as light, with far less wasted as heat. An LED bulb can therefore produce the same amount of light as an old bulb while using less than a fifth of the electricity. Because there is no hot wire to wear thin, many LED bulbs are expected to last fifteen thousand hours or more.

This does not mean that LEDs stay cool. The electronics in the base of an LED bulb still produce some heat, and heat shortens their working life. For this reason, many LED bulbs have metal fins or a metal base that carries warmth away, and they may fail early if they are fitted inside a closed lamp where hot air is trapped.

The first LEDs gave off only red light, and later ones added yellow and green, which is why they were used mainly in the small indicator lights on machines. A bright white LED became practical only after engineers developed efficient blue LEDs. Most white LED bulbs today use a blue LED covered with a thin coating that changes part of the blue light into yellow. Our eyes see the mixture as white.

The change has also affected the way people shop. For decades, customers chose bulbs by their wattage, which measures how much electricity a bulb uses, and treated that number as a measure of brightness. With the old technology the shortcut worked, because a 100-watt bulb was reliably brighter than a 40-watt one. With LEDs it fails: a bulb that gives as much light as the old 60-watt type may use only eight or nine watts. Packages therefore now show lumens, a unit for the amount of light a bulb actually produces. Shoppers have had to learn to read a number that was always the real answer to their question.

items.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: New technology has made many everyday objects in the home cheaper, safer and easier to use.
White LED bulbs use a blue light with a coating that turns part of it into yellow.
LEDs give off more heat than old bulbs, which is why they burn out much sooner.
LEDs waste far less energy as heat than old bulbs, which has changed how bulbs are chosen.
items.correct_answer: LEDs waste far less energy as heat than old bulbs, which has changed how bulbs are chosen.
items.why: energy is released directly as light, with far less wasted as heat
items.explanation: "LEDs waste far less energy as heat than old bulbs, which has changed how bulbs are chosen." is correct: the passage contrasts old bulbs, where "roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat", with LEDs, where "energy is released directly as light, with far less wasted as heat", and ends with how "The change has also affected the way people shop".

distractor_rationales.choice: New technology has made many everyday objects in the home cheaper, safer and easier to use.
distractor_rationales.reason: "New technology has made many everyday objects in the home cheaper, safer and easier to use." is too general: the passage is about one object, the light bulb, and about how "LEDs, work in a completely different way".

distractor_rationales.choice: White LED bulbs use a blue light with a coating that turns part of it into yellow.
distractor_rationales.reason: "White LED bulbs use a blue light with a coating that turns part of it into yellow." is one detail from paragraph 5 ("a blue LED covered with a thin coating"), not the point of the whole passage.

distractor_rationales.choice: LEDs give off more heat than old bulbs, which is why they burn out much sooner.
distractor_rationales.reason: "LEDs give off more heat than old bulbs, which is why they burn out much sooner." gets the comparison backwards: LEDs release light "with far less wasted as heat", and they are "expected to last fifteen thousand hours or more" against "about a thousand hours" for old bulbs.

items.prompt: Why did an old light bulb eventually stop working?
choices: Its wire slowly lost metal and grew thin until it snapped.
Its glass slowly turned dark until little light got out.
Its glass cracked when cool air touched the hot surface.
Its wire suddenly melted when the current became too strong.
items.correct_answer: Its wire slowly lost metal and grew thin until it snapped.
items.why: tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire, so the filament became thinner in places until it finally broke
items.explanation: "Its wire slowly lost metal and grew thin until it snapped." is correct: the passage says "tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire, so the filament became thinner in places until it finally broke".

distractor_rationales.choice: Its glass slowly turned dark until little light got out.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Its glass slowly turned dark until little light got out." is wrong: the passage gives a different cause, that "the filament became thinner in places until it finally broke".

distractor_rationales.choice: Its glass cracked when cool air touched the hot surface.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Its glass cracked when cool air touched the hot surface." is wrong: the passage gives a different cause, in the wire, not the glass: "tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire".

distractor_rationales.choice: Its wire suddenly melted when the current became too strong.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Its wire suddenly melted when the current became too strong." is wrong: the wire failed gradually, as "tiny amounts of tungsten slowly escaped from the surface of the wire".

items.prompt: All of the following are stated about LED bulbs EXCEPT:
choices: They need much less electricity than old bulbs for the same light.
Their light slowly becomes weaker as the bulbs grow older.
Their white light comes from mixing blue light with yellow made by a coating.
Their packages now give the amount of light they produce in lumens.
items.correct_answer: Their light slowly becomes weaker as the bulbs grow older.
items.explanation: "Their light slowly becomes weaker as the bulbs grow older." is correct: the passage discusses how long LED bulbs work ("expected to last fifteen thousand hours or more"; "heat shortens their working life"; "they may fail early"), but it says nothing about their light growing weaker with age.

distractor_rationales.choice: They need much less electricity than old bulbs for the same light.
distractor_rationales.reason: "They need much less electricity than old bulbs for the same light." is stated: an LED bulb gives "the same amount of light as an old bulb while using less than a fifth of the electricity".

distractor_rationales.choice: Their white light comes from mixing blue light with yellow made by a coating.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Their white light comes from mixing blue light with yellow made by a coating." is stated: white LED bulbs "use a blue LED covered with a thin coating that changes part of the blue light into yellow".

distractor_rationales.choice: Their packages now give the amount of light they produce in lumens.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Their packages now give the amount of light they produce in lumens." is stated: "Packages therefore now show lumens, a unit for the amount of light a bulb actually produces".

items.prompt: It can be inferred that choosing old bulbs by their wattage worked mainly because
choices: wattage was a direct measure of the light that each bulb gave off
all the old bulbs produced very little heat compared with their light
all the old bulbs turned electricity into light in much the same way
the old bulbs used a semiconductor that released energy directly as light

items.explanation: "all the old bulbs turned electricity into light in much the same way" is correct: every old bulb made light the same way, as "an electric current passed through a thin wire called a filament", so more electricity meant more light: "With the old technology the shortcut worked, because a 100-watt bulb was reliably brighter than a 40-watt one". When LEDs "work in a completely different way", the shortcut fails.

distractor_rationales.reason: "all the old bulbs produced very little heat compared with their light" is contradicted: in old bulbs "roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat rather than as visible light".

distractor_rationales.choice: the old bulbs used a semiconductor that released energy directly as light
distractor_rationales.reason: "the old bulbs used a semiconductor that released energy directly as light" is contradicted: old bulbs used "a thin wire called a filament"; the semiconductor is how "LEDs, work in a completely different way".

items.prompt: Why does the writer mention touching a lamp that was switched on an hour earlier?
choices: to warn readers that old lamps can cause serious burns to the skin
to explain why the filament inside old bulbs was made of tungsten
to show that LED bulbs are much safer to touch than old bulbs
to give an everyday example of how much heat old bulbs produced
items.correct_answer: to give an everyday example of how much heat old bulbs produced
items.why: Anyone who has touched a lamp that was switched on an hour earlier has learned this quickly
items.explanation: "to give an everyday example of how much heat old bulbs produced" is correct: the sentence "Anyone who has touched a lamp that was switched on an hour earlier has learned this quickly" comes right after "most of the energy, roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat", and gives a familiar example of that heat.

distractor_rationales.choice: to warn readers that old lamps can cause serious burns to the skin
distractor_rationales.reason: "to warn readers that old lamps can cause serious burns to the skin" is wrong: the sentence follows the claim that "roughly ninety percent, left the bulb as heat", and illustrates it; the passage gives readers no safety advice.

distractor_rationales.choice: to explain why the filament inside old bulbs was made of tungsten
distractor_rationales.reason: "to explain why the filament inside old bulbs was made of tungsten" is wrong: tungsten is only named as the usual material ("usually made of the metal tungsten"); the lamp sentence comes after the point about heat.

distractor_rationales.choice: to show that LED bulbs are much safer to touch than old bulbs
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that LED bulbs are much safer to touch than old bulbs" is wrong: LEDs are not discussed until paragraph 3, and paragraph 4 says "This does not mean that LEDs stay cool".

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 4?
choices: to warn that LED bulbs can still be harmed by their own heat
to explain why LED bulbs use less electricity than old bulbs
to describe how a white light is made from a blue LED
to show that LED bulbs last much longer than the old bulbs
items.correct_answer: to warn that LED bulbs can still be harmed by their own heat
items.why: This does not mean that LEDs stay cool
items.explanation: "to warn that LED bulbs can still be harmed by their own heat" is correct: paragraph 4 opens with "This does not mean that LEDs stay cool" and explains that "heat shortens their working life" and "they may fail early if they are fitted inside a closed lamp where hot air is trapped".

distractor_rationales.choice: to explain why LED bulbs use less electricity than old bulbs
distractor_rationales.reason: "to explain why LED bulbs use less electricity than old bulbs" is wrong: that is the work of paragraph 3 ("using less than a fifth of the electricity"); paragraph 4 is about how "heat shortens their working life".

distractor_rationales.choice: to describe how a white light is made from a blue LED
distractor_rationales.reason: "to describe how a white light is made from a blue LED" is wrong: that is paragraph 5 ("a blue LED covered with a thin coating"); paragraph 4 is about heat in the bulb's base.

distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that LED bulbs last much longer than the old bulbs" is wrong: the long life is given in paragraph 3 ("fifteen thousand hours or more"); paragraph 4 explains why "they may fail early".
